senses.gloss: Trying to do more than is realistic.
examples: The schedule was *overambitious* from the start.
He's an *overambitious* young manager who promises too much.
Six cities in four days sounds *overambitious* to me.

senses.gloss: Worrying much more than the situation calls for.
examples: *Overanxious* parents call the coach after every game.
Don't be *overanxious* about the results.
She gets *overanxious* whenever the phone rings late.

senses.gloss: Trying to control everyone around you, in a way people resent.
examples: His *overbearing* boss checks every email he sends.
She can be *overbearing* when she's stressed.
The most *overbearing* teacher I ever had made us stand to answer.

senses.gloss: Made to seem much bigger or more serious than it is.
examples: The threat turned out to be *overblown*.
It was an *overblown* story that the papers loved.
His praise was *overblown*, but she enjoyed it anyway.

senses.gloss: Carrying far more work, debt or responsibility than is reasonable.
examples: The court system is *overburdened* with small cases.
*Overburdened* nurses are leaving the profession.
She felt *overburdened* by debt after the move.

contrast: Only of the sky or the weather. A person in a dark mood is *gloomy*, never *overcast*.

senses.gloss: Covered with cloud.
examples: It was gray and *overcast* all weekend.
We took the photo on an *overcast* day, so there were no shadows.
The sky stayed *overcast* until noon.

senses.gloss: So careful that you miss chances or slow everything down.
examples: The bank was *overcautious* and lost the deal.
*Overcautious* drivers can cause accidents too.
I'd rather be *overcautious* than sorry.

senses.gloss: Too sure of yourself, and careless because of it.
examples: The team got *overconfident* after two easy wins.
He's *overconfident* about passing without studying.
An *overconfident* answer is worse than an honest 'I don't know'.

senses.gloss: Finding fault far more than is fair or useful.
examples: Try not to be *overcritical* of your own writing.
He had an *overcritical* editor who rewrote every line.
Her father was *overcritical*, and she still hears his voice.

position: both — the food sense usually after a verb

senses.gloss: Cooked too long.
examples: The steak was *overdone* and dry.
I like my eggs soft, not *overdone*.

senses.gloss: Done so heavily that it stops being convincing.
examples: The decorations were a little *overdone*.
His surprise looked *overdone* to everyone at the table.

senses.gloss: Dressed more formally than the occasion calls for.
examples: I felt *overdressed* in a suit at a backyard party.
Better *overdressed* than underdressed, my mother says.
She was the most *overdressed* person in the room.

position: both — mostly after a verb; before a noun in *an overdue book*
comparison: not gradable — *long overdue* is the usual intensifier

senses.gloss: Not paid or returned by the date it was due.
examples: The rent is two weeks *overdue*.
I finally returned an *overdue* library book.

senses.gloss: Needed long ago and still not done.
examples: This conversation is long *overdue*.
An apology was *overdue* by then.

senses.gloss: So keen to do something that you push too hard.
examples: The *overeager* salesman followed us around the store.
He was *overeager* to prove himself on the first day.
Don't be *overeager*; let them come to you.

senses.gloss: Showing much stronger feelings than the moment calls for.
examples: I got *overemotional* at the airport and cried.
He called the speech *overemotional* and short on facts.
She's the *most overemotional* one in the family, and she knows it.

senses.gloss: Excited about something to a degree that tires other people out.
examples: An *overenthusiastic* waiter described every dish twice.
I may have been *overenthusiastic* about the idea.
The *overenthusiastic* cheering drowned out the singer.

senses.gloss: So excited that you cannot settle down or think clearly.
examples: The kids were *overexcited* about the trip and couldn't sleep.
Don't get *overexcited* — it's only the first round.
*Overexcited* dogs jump on guests.

senses.gloss: So full that the contents are coming over the edge.
examples: The trash can was *overflowing*.
She came in with an *overflowing* bag of groceries.
He was *overflowing* with ideas after the trip.

senses.gloss: Covered with plants that have grown wild.
examples: The back yard is *overgrown* with weeds.
We followed an *overgrown* path down to the lake.

senses.gloss: Too big for what it really is, often of an adult acting like a child.
examples: He's an *overgrown* kid with a company credit card.
The town is really just an *overgrown* village.

position: attributive only — after a verb the word is the adverb: *A plane flew overhead*
contrast: The adjective is stressed OH-vur-hed; the adverb (*flew overhead*) is oh-vur-HED. *Overhead* is also a noun for running costs: *We cut our overhead*.

senses.gloss: Above your head.
examples: Put your bag in the *overhead* bin.
The *overhead* lights buzzed all night.

senses.gloss: Of the everyday running costs of a business.
examples: We cut our *overhead* costs by giving up the office.
*Overhead* expenses ate most of the profit.

senses.gloss: Made too hot.
examples: The car sat on the shoulder with an *overheated* engine.
The room was *overheated* and stuffy.

senses.gloss: Too excited or too active, of an argument or a market.
examples: The debate got *overheated* fast.
Economists are warning about an *overheated* housing market.

ru: вне себя от радости, очень обрадованный
position: predicative only — never before a noun: say *a delighted child*

senses.gloss: Extremely happy about something.
examples: We were *overjoyed* at the news.
She was *overjoyed* to see her brother at the gate.
They were *overjoyed* that the surgery went well.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the adverb: *They traveled overland*

senses.gloss: Going across land rather than by sea or air.
examples: They took the *overland* route through Turkey.
An *overland* journey from Cairo to Cape Town takes months.
*Overland* shipping is slower but cheaper than air.

senses.gloss: Carrying more weight, current or work than it was built for.
examples: The truck was *overloaded* and tipped on the curve.
An *overloaded* outlet started the fire.
I'm *overloaded* with work this month.

senses.gloss: Not noticed or not given the attention it deserves.
examples: Sleep is the most *overlooked* part of training.
An easily *overlooked* detail cost them the case.
Her early novels were *overlooked* for years.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the adverb: *We stayed overnight*
contrast: The adjective is stressed OH-vur-nyt; the adverb (*drove overnight*) is oh-vur-NYT.

senses.gloss: Lasting or happening during the night.
examples: We took the *overnight* train to Chicago.
Pack an *overnight* bag and nothing more.

senses.gloss: Happening suddenly, as if in a single night.
examples: The band was an *overnight* success after ten years in bars.
There is no *overnight* fix for this.

senses.gloss: So strong that you cannot resist it or ignore it.
examples: The smell of gasoline was *overpowering*.
She felt an *overpowering* urge to walk out.
His cologne is *overpowering* in a small room.

senses.gloss: Costing much more than it is worth.
examples: The coffee here is wildly *overpriced*.
We walked out of an *overpriced* tourist restaurant.
Nothing is *more overpriced* than airport water.

senses.gloss: Guarding someone so closely that you hold them back.
examples: My parents were *overprotective* of their youngest.
She's an *overprotective* dog owner, and she admits it.
He got *more overprotective* after the accident.

senses.gloss: Going further than your power, right or ability really allows.
examples: The court struck down the *overreaching* rule.
Critics called the plan *overreaching* and expensive.
An *overreaching* landlord can lose in court.

position: attributive only — *Her overriding concern was safety*, never *Her concern was overriding*

senses.gloss: More important than everything else.
examples: Safety was the *overriding* concern.
My *overriding* memory of that summer is the heat.
There is no *overriding* reason to change the date.

senses.gloss: Left so long that it has gone soft and started to spoil.
examples: The bananas are *overripe*, so let's make bread.
He bit into an *overripe* peach and juice ran down his arm.
Nothing smells worse than *overripe* melon in a hot car.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the adverb: *She lives overseas*

senses.gloss: In or from a country across the ocean.
examples: Most of our *overseas* customers pay in dollars.
He took an *overseas* assignment in Singapore.
*Overseas* travel got cheaper that year.

senses.gloss: Reacting far more strongly than the situation calls for.
examples: Don't be *oversensitive* about a joke.
My skin is *oversensitive* to sunscreen.
An *oversensitive* smoke alarm goes off every time I cook.

position: attributive only — after a verb use *oversized*
contrast: *Oversize* and *oversized* mean the same thing. *Oversize* is the form on road signs and shipping labels; *oversized* is the everyday one.

senses.gloss: Bigger than the standard size.
examples: The truck carried an *oversize* load.
Airlines charge extra for *oversize* baggage.
He wore an *oversize* coat that hid his hands.

senses.gloss: Much bigger than usual, sometimes on purpose.
examples: She sleeps in an *oversized* T-shirt.
The chair looked *oversized* in the small room.
*Oversized* sunglasses were back in style that spring.

position: both — very often in *cannot be overstated*

senses.gloss: Described as bigger or more certain than the facts support.
examples: The importance of sleep cannot be *overstated*.
His role in the project was *overstated*.
Those were *overstated* claims, and the regulators said so.

ru: набитый до отказа; мягкий и пухлый (о мебели)

senses.gloss: Filled far too full.
examples: She dragged an *overstuffed* suitcase up the stairs.
My closet is *overstuffed* and I can't shut it.

senses.gloss: Of furniture: thickly padded and soft.
examples: He fell asleep in an *overstuffed* armchair.
The lobby had *overstuffed* sofas and bad lamps.

position: both — almost always before a noun
contrast: *Overt* is done in the open; *covert* is hidden. Americans stress it oh-VURT, not OH-vurt.

senses.gloss: Done openly, where anyone can see it.
examples: There was no *overt* threat, just a look.
*Overt* discrimination is easier to prove than the quiet kind.
Their support became *more overt* after the vote.

senses.gloss: Turned upside down.
examples: An *overturned* truck blocked two lanes.
The boat lay *overturned* on the beach.

senses.gloss: Of a decision: canceled by a higher authority.
examples: The *overturned* conviction made the evening news.
The ruling was *overturned* on appeal.

position: attributive only — with a small set of nouns: *pride*, *ambition*, *confidence*
contrast: Formal and literary, and it describes the feeling, not the person: *overweening pride*, not *an overweening man*.

senses.gloss: Far too great, of pride or ambition.
examples: His *overweening* pride cost him the friendship.
*Overweening* ambition brought the company down.
She wrote about the *overweening* confidence of young traders.

ru: имеющий лишний вес, полный; сверхнормативный (о багаже)
position: both — of people almost always after a verb: *He is overweight*
contrast: Of a person this is the neutral word; *fat* is blunt and often rude. Of luggage it simply means too heavy.

senses.gloss: Heavier than is healthy, of a person or an animal.
examples: The doctor said he was slightly *overweight*.
Their cat is *overweight* and lazy.

senses.gloss: Heavier than the limit allowed.
examples: They charged me for an *overweight* bag.
An *overweight* truck pays a fine at the scales.

senses.gloss: Very upset and unable to calm down.
examples: She was too *overwrought* to drive home.
He gets *overwrought* before every exam.

senses.gloss: Of writing or art: too elaborate and too worked over.
examples: The prose is *overwrought* and hard to finish.
It's an *overwrought* ending to a quiet movie.

senses.gloss: Doing a job with far more energy than it needs, and doing harm that way.
examples: An *overzealous* editor cut half the chapter.
The guards were *overzealous* about checking bags.
Don't be *overzealous* with the salt.

ru: совиный, как у совы (о виде, очках)

senses.gloss: Looking like an owl: round glasses, wide eyes, a solemn stare.
examples: He peered at us with an *owlish* look over his glasses.
Her round *owlish* frames made her look older.
The professor was small, gray and *owlish*.

position: attributive only — always after a possessive: *my own room*, *the city's own bus line*
contrast: *Own* never stands alone: *my own car*, never *an own car* — the usual mistake for Russian *свой*. It also comes after the noun in *a place of my own*. The verb *own* (*She owns the building*) is a different word.

senses.gloss: Belonging to that person and to nobody else.
examples: She has her *own* room now.
I'd like a place of my *own*.
They grow their *own* vegetables.

contrast: With a capital it means the ocean. Lowercase *pacific* is a formal word for peaceful (*a pacific gesture*), and it is rare in speech.

senses.gloss: Of the Pacific Ocean or the lands around it.
examples: We drove up the *Pacific* coast from San Diego.
*Pacific* storms hit Oregon first.
She studies *Pacific* island languages.

contrast: Much more often a noun: *She's a pacifist*. As an adjective it describes beliefs, families and movements.

senses.gloss: Opposed to war and to violence on principle.
examples: He came from a *pacifist* family.
*Pacifist* groups organized the march.
Her politics are firmly *pacifist*.

senses.gloss: Sold in a box, bag or wrapper rather than loose.
examples: *Packaged* foods list the salt on the side of the box.
We buy *packaged* rice because it keeps longer.

senses.gloss: Sold as one deal with everything included.
examples: They booked a *packaged* tour of Italy.
It's a *packaged* deal: hotel, car and flights.

ru: мягкий, с подкладкой; раздутый (о счёте, резюме)

senses.gloss: With soft material inside for comfort or protection.
examples: She sat on a *padded* bench by the window.
The jacket is *padded* at the shoulders.

senses.gloss: Made bigger by adding things that do not belong there.
examples: The bill was *padded* with fees nobody explained.
He turned in a *padded* resume and got caught.

contrast: Also a noun (*the pagans of northern Europe*). Capitalized *Pagan* usually means the living modern religion; lowercase points to the pre-Christian world.

senses.gloss: Belonging to an old religion that came before Christianity, or to modern nature worship.
examples: Many Christmas customs have *pagan* roots.
The museum has a room of *pagan* statues.
Her grandmother called the festival *pagan* and refused to go.

comparison: not gradable — but compounds compare: *better paid*, *the best-paid job in town*

senses.gloss: That you receive money for.
examples: She took a *paid* internship in Denver.
We get ten days of *paid* leave a year.

senses.gloss: Already settled, of a bill or an account.
examples: The invoice is *paid* in full.
Mark the account *paid* and file it.

senses.gloss: Feeling no pain, or causing none.
examples: Two weeks after surgery she was finally *pain-free*.
They advertise a *pain-free* dental visit.
No treatment is completely *pain-free*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a pained expression*
contrast: *Pained* shows hurt feelings on a face; *painful* causes pain. A *pained* smile hurts nobody; a *painful* shot does.

senses.gloss: Showing that you are hurt, upset or embarrassed.
examples: He gave me a *pained* smile and changed the subject.
There was a *pained* silence after the question.
She looked *pained* when I mentioned his name.

contrast: A thing that hurts you is *painful*; a face that shows hurt is *pained*.

senses.gloss: Hurting the body.
examples: The shot was quick but *painful*.
He has a *painful* knee and won't see anyone about it.

senses.gloss: Hard to go through, to remember or to watch.
examples: It was a *painful* conversation for both of them.
Losing that game was *more painful* than the whole season.

senses.gloss: Causing no physical pain.
examples: The procedure is quick and *painless*.
They promised a *painless* shot, and it was.

senses.gloss: Easy, with no trouble or effort.
examples: Moving the files over was *painless*.
There is no *painless* way to fire someone.

position: both — almost always before a noun

senses.gloss: Done slowly and with great care for every detail.
examples: The restoration was slow, *painstaking* work.
She kept *painstaking* notes of every call.
It took *painstaking* research to find the name.

senses.gloss: Covered or decorated with paint.
examples: The *painted* door was still sticky.
She bought a hand-*painted* bowl in Oaxaca.
The walls are *painted* a soft gray.

position: both — *a Pakistani restaurant*, *Her parents are Pakistani*
contrast: Also a noun (*two Pakistanis*), but *a Pakistani woman* is the safer wording for a person.

senses.gloss: Of or from Pakistan, its people or its culture.
examples: We went to a *Pakistani* restaurant on Devon Avenue.
Her parents are *Pakistani*.
*Pakistani* mangoes reach the stores in June.

senses.gloss: Good enough to eat or drink.
examples: The soup was bland but *palatable*.
A little lemon makes it *more palatable*.

senses.gloss: Acceptable to people, of an idea or a decision.
examples: They rewrote the bill to make it *palatable* to both parties.
By then there was no *palatable* option left.

senses.gloss: Very large and grand, like a palace.
examples: They rented a *palatial* house on the lake.
The lobby is *palatial*, all marble and gold.
It's the *most palatial* hotel in the state.

contrast: American spelling *Paleolithic*; British books print *Palaeolithic*.

senses.gloss: Of the earliest and longest part of the Stone Age.
examples: The cave holds *Paleolithic* paintings.
*Paleolithic* tools were chipped, not polished.
He teaches a course on *Paleolithic* Europe.

senses.gloss: Of or from Palestine, or of the Palestinian people.
examples: A *Palestinian* poet read at the festival.
Her mother is *Palestinian*.
*Palestinian* families have lived in the camp for decades.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *palliative care*
contrast: Also a noun (*a palliative*). *Palliative care* eases symptoms; it does not try to cure the disease.

senses.gloss: Easing pain or symptoms without curing the cause.
examples: She moved into *palliative* care in the spring.
The drug is *palliative*, not a cure.
They offered only *palliative* measures.

senses.gloss: So strong that you can almost touch it, of a feeling in a room.
examples: The tension in the room was *palpable*.
There was a *palpable* sense of relief when he walked in.

senses.gloss: In medicine: that a doctor can feel with the hands.
examples: The lump was *palpable* on the left side.
The doctor found no *palpable* swelling.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a paltry sum*

senses.gloss: Embarrassingly small, of an amount or an offer.
examples: They offered a *paltry* two percent raise.
He sold the painting for a *paltry* sum.
The second offer was even *paltrier* than the first.

senses.gloss: Of or from Panama.
examples: A *Panamanian* crew ran the boat.
His wife is *Panamanian*.
*Panamanian* coffee is hard to find here.

senses.gloss: Of the pancreas.
examples: *Pancreatic* cancer is hard to catch early.
The scan showed a *pancreatic* cyst.
He takes *pancreatic* enzymes with every meal.

contrast: These days far more often a noun: *during the pandemic*. An *epidemic* stays in one region; a *pandemic* crosses countries.

senses.gloss: Of a disease that has spread across many countries.
examples: *Pandemic* flu spreads faster than the seasonal kind.
The virus reached *pandemic* levels in three months.
Officials still describe the outbreak as *pandemic*.

position: both — mostly before a noun, and often in compounds: *wood-paneled*
contrast: American *paneled* with one *l*; British books print *panelled*.

senses.gloss: Covered with flat boards of wood on the walls.
examples: He works in a dark, *paneled* study.
The walls are *paneled* in oak.
They drove a wood-*paneled* station wagon.

senses.gloss: Suddenly so frightened that you cannot think.
examples: *Panic-stricken* shoppers ran for the doors.
She called me, *panic-stricken*, at two in the morning.
He was *panic-stricken* when he couldn't find his passport.

form: -ed from *panic* — a *k* is added before the ending
contrast: Watch the spelling: *panicked*, *panicking*, both with a *k*.

senses.gloss: Filled with sudden fear, or showing it.
examples: A *panicked* crowd pushed toward the exit.
She sent a *panicked* text about the deadline.
I was too *panicked* to think straight.

senses.gloss: Beginning to panic, or easily made to panic.
examples: I get *panicky* in crowds.
Don't send a *panicky* email at midnight.
The market turned *panicky* after the announcement.

senses.gloss: Taking in a wide view in every direction.
examples: The room has a *panoramic* view of the bay.
He took a *panoramic* photo from the roof.
*Panoramic* windows run the length of the restaurant.

senses.gloss: Of the pope.
examples: The *papal* visit filled the square.
She quoted a *papal* letter from 1963.
*Papal* elections are held behind closed doors.

senses.gloss: True and self-contradictory at the same time.
examples: It's *paradoxical* that the safer car makes people drive faster.
She has a *paradoxical* love of rules and of breaking them.
The result seems *paradoxical* until you read the footnote.

senses.gloss: Of or from Paraguay.
examples: A *Paraguayan* harpist opened the concert.
Her husband is *Paraguayan*.
*Paraguayan* beef is sold all over the region.

contrast: Watch the spelling: one *r*, then two *l*s, then one. It is also a noun (*draw a parallel*) and a verb (*Her story parallels his*).

senses.gloss: Running side by side, always the same distance apart.
examples: The street runs *parallel* to the river.
Draw two *parallel* lines an inch apart.

senses.gloss: Similar and happening at the same time.
examples: The two investigations were *parallel* but separate.
He led a *parallel* life in another city.

contrast: American *paralyzed*; British books print *paralysed*.

senses.gloss: Unable to move part or all of the body.
examples: He was *paralyzed* from the waist down after the crash.
Her left arm is *paralyzed*.

senses.gloss: Unable to act or to function at all.
examples: I was *paralyzed* with fear and just stood there.
The strike left the airport *paralyzed* for two days.

senses.gloss: Organized and armed like an army, but not part of the official one.
examples: A *paramilitary* group controlled the border.
They wore *paramilitary* uniforms without insignia.
*Paramilitary* training camps operated there for years.

senses.gloss: More important than anything else.
examples: Safety is *paramount* on the job site.
The question is of *paramount* importance.
For her, family is *paramount*.

contrast: In everyday talk it just means far too suspicious (*paranoid about locking the door*); in medicine it names a serious condition, so it is worth keeping the joking use for small worries.

senses.gloss: Wrongly convinced that people are out to harm you, or simply far too suspicious.
examples: I'm *paranoid* about leaving the stove on.
He got *paranoid* after reading the comments.
She's the *most paranoid* person I know about passwords.

senses.gloss: Of events that science cannot explain, like ghosts or telepathy.
examples: She writes *paranormal* romance novels.
The show investigates *paranormal* activity in old hotels.
Nothing about the noise was *paranormal* — it was the pipes.

contrast: Also a noun, but many people prefer *a paraplegic man* or *a man with paraplegia* to *a paraplegic*.

senses.gloss: Unable to move the legs and the lower body.
examples: He has been *paraplegic* since the accident.
The center trains *paraplegic* athletes.
*Paraplegic* patients relearn how to get around.

senses.gloss: Living on or inside another living thing and feeding off it.
examples: *Parasitic* worms are common in the region.
The plant is *parasitic* and takes water from the tree.

senses.gloss: Living off other people's work or money.
examples: He called the middlemen *parasitic*.
It's a *parasitic* business model and everyone knows it.

senses.gloss: Very dry, of land, lips or a throat.
examples: The fields were *parched* after two months without rain.
My lips were *parched* from the wind.

senses.gloss: Informal: very thirsty.
examples: I'm *parched* — is there any water?
After the hike we were all *parched*.

senses.gloss: Of a parent or of parents.
examples: *Parental* consent is required for the trip.
The app has *parental* controls.
She took *parental* leave in March.

senses.gloss: Added as an aside, in brackets or between commas.
examples: He added a *parenthetical* note about the source.
Her *parenthetical* remark turned out to be the whole point.
The comment was *parenthetical* and got cut.

senses.gloss: Of or from Paris.
examples: We stayed in a tiny *Parisian* apartment.
Her accent is unmistakably *Parisian*.
*Parisian* cafes fill up after six.

position: both — before a noun (*a parked car*); after *be* it is usually the passive: *The car is parked outside*

senses.gloss: Standing where it was left, of a vehicle.
examples: A *parked* car blocked the driveway.
The truck is *parked* around the corner.
She hit a *parked* van backing out.

contrast: The middle is pronounced pahr-luh-, not pahr-lee-uh-, even though the spelling shows *-lia-*.

senses.gloss: Of a parliament or of the way one works.
examples: Canada has a *parliamentary* system.
The *parliamentary* election is set for June.
He knows every *parliamentary* rule by heart.

senses.gloss: Of a church parish, especially of a parish school.
examples: She went to a *parochial* school in Boston.
Most *parochial* schools charge tuition.

senses.gloss: Interested only in your own small corner of the world.
examples: His view of the country is pretty *parochial*.
The debate was *parochial* and missed the larger question.

contrast: Formal and a little bookish. In speech Americans say *cheap* or *stingy*.

senses.gloss: Unwilling to spend or to give, even when there is plenty.
examples: The company is *parsimonious* with raises.
He kept a *parsimonious* household on a very good salary.
She's *more parsimonious* than poor.

comparison: not gradable — except in the third sense: *more partial to sweets*
takes: *to* + noun or *-ing*, in the third sense

senses.gloss: Not complete.
examples: We got a *partial* refund.
They have only a *partial* list of names.

senses.gloss: Favoring one side instead of judging fairly.
examples: A judge must not be *partial*.
The report was *partial*, and everyone in the room knew it.

senses.gloss: Fond of something.
examples: I'm *partial* to dark chocolate.
He's *partial* to old westerns.

senses.gloss: Taking part in a program or an offer, of a business or a school.
examples: The offer is good at *participating* locations only.
*Participating* pharmacies give the shot for free.
A list of *participating* schools is on the website.

ru: основанный на участии, с участием людей

senses.gloss: Built so that ordinary people take part in the decisions.
examples: The city tried *participatory* budgeting.
It's a *participatory* museum, and you touch everything.
*Participatory* democracy takes more time than voting once a year.

contrast: A false friend. In American political news a *partisan* is a party loyalist, not a *партизан*; the fighter sense survives mostly in history writing. Also a noun.

senses.gloss: Strongly supporting one political party, often blindly.
examples: The vote was strictly *partisan*.
Washington has gotten *more partisan* every year.

senses.gloss: Of irregular fighters resisting an occupying army.
examples: He wrote a history of *partisan* warfare in Yugoslavia.
*Partisan* units operated out of the forests.

senses.gloss: Good enough, but no better than that.
examples: He speaks *passable* Spanish.
The food was *passable* and the view was great.

senses.gloss: That you can travel on or through.
examples: The road is *passable* again now that the plows came through.
Only one bridge was still *passable*.

position: predicative only — almost always after a verb: *That style is passé*
form: from French; American writing usually keeps the accent: *passé*

senses.gloss: No longer fashionable.
examples: Those jeans are *passé*.
He said email was *passé*, which surprised the room.
Calling it a blog feels a little *passé* now.

position: attributive only — *a passing remark*, *a passing grade*

senses.gloss: Lasting only a moment, or done quickly and without much attention.
examples: He made a *passing* remark about moving.
She had a *passing* interest in chess and then dropped it.

senses.gloss: Good enough to pass a test or a class.
examples: A 70 is a *passing* grade.
He needs a *passing* score to graduate.

senses.gloss: Feeling or showing very strong emotion.
examples: They had a *passionate* argument about the budget.
She gave a *passionate* speech to the council.

senses.gloss: Caring very much about something you do.
examples: He's *passionate* about teaching.
I've never met anyone *more passionate* about birds.
